claims.text: Exposed active surfaces of transition-metal catalysts are susceptible to sintering under reaction conditions.
Exposed active surfaces of transition-metal catalysts are susceptible to oxidation under reaction conditions.
A thin, conformal oxide coating improves transition-metal catalyst durability.
A thin, conformal oxide coating improves transition-metal catalyst selectivity.
The oxide coating stabilizes active surface sites.
The oxide coating modulates local oxidation states.
The oxide coating retards catalyst sintering at high temperatures.
The oxide coating forms a stable protective layer.
The protective layer limits surface-atom migration.
The protective oxide layer acts as a barrier that inhibits metal-particle agglomeration.
Stabilization of surface oxidation states preserves active catalytic sites.
Controlled surface chemistry produced by the coating can improve selectivity.
Coated catalysts will deactivate more slowly than uncoated catalysts under identical high-temperature conditions.
Coated catalysts may exhibit improved selectivity relative to uncoated catalysts.
The proposed benefit is expected only when sintering is a dominant degradation mode and active-site stability is important.
A coating that significantly obstructs reactant access may eliminate the proposed benefit.
The magnitude of improvement depends on oxide identity, coating thickness, catalyst composition, and reaction environment.

contradictions.description: The headline hypothesis asserts improved selectivity, whereas the predicted outcome describes selectivity improvement as only potential. The falsification rule can reject the hypothesis for no selectivity improvement, making an uncertain secondary prediction function as a required outcome.
